overview: Thursday's session was shaped by three events: the trilateral summit outcome in Shenzhen, Anthropic's blockbuster Nasdaq debut, and a fresh escalation in the Strait of Hormuz. The unprecedented Trump–Xi–Putin summit produced a symbolic 'peace declaration' committing to nuclear risk reduction and dialogue — a diplomatic milestone — but yielded no concrete deliverables on Hormuz, Ukraine, or the November 27 critical minerals deadline, now 7 days away. The market verdict was swift: gold fell for a ninth straight session to $3,648 per ounce, down 2.0%, extending its worst losing streak in over a year as the dollar held near 19-month highs and December rate-hike odds remained at 95%. Brent crude rebounded 2.0% to $92.00 per barrel after Iran's IRGC planted mines on two tankers transiting the American-backed southern route — the most provocative Hormuz escalation in weeks — though WTI slipped 1.9% to $82.50 as the EIA confirmed a large crude inventory build. Silver eased 1.7% to $44.44; platinum dipped 0.7% to $1,347; palladium fell 2.0% to $916. Copper dropped 2.4% to $5.61 per pound on continued dollar pressure and DRC logistics disruption. Newcastle coal held at $150, sustained by winter demand. Wheat rebounded 1.2% to 577 cents after consecutive days of selling; corn edged down 0.6% to 433 cents; soybeans eased 0.4%. Cocoa rebounded 2.8% to $5,169 on renewed West African supply concerns.

Anthropic (ANT) opened at $83 and surged to close at $97 on its first day of Nasdaq trading — a 17% pop that made it the strongest major-tech IPO debut since SpaceX. The stock briefly touched $102 intraday before settling. Bitcoin recovered 2.2% to approximately $63,800 as crypto markets rebounded from oversold levels following Wednesday's 200-week moving average breakdown; Ethereum rose 2.8% to $1,802; the Fear and Greed Index ticked up from Extreme Fear. The Hormuz mine incident escalated tensions despite the summit — three US carrier strike groups remain in the Persian Gulf and Iran's IRGC warned of further actions. Base metals were mixed: nickel fell 1.2% to $15,665 on LME, zinc rose 0.9% to $3,562, and tin dropped 4.4% to approximately $43,500. The LNG JKM front-month contract rolled from November to December, with the new front-month around $27.50 per MMBtu — the decline from $33 reflects the contract rollover rather than a fundamental price shift. The November 27 gallium, germanium and antimony deadline is now 7 days away with no progress from the summit, leaving markets to price in the growing probability that China's export bans resume next week.

watchItems.title: November 27 gallium, germanium and antimony deadline now 7 days away — summit produced no progress
watchItems.text: The November 27 deadline for China's US-specific export-control suspension on gallium, germanium and antimony is now 7 days away. Thursday's trilateral summit in Shenzhen — the last major diplomatic window — produced no visible progress on critical minerals. China produces approximately 99% of global gallium, 60–80% of germanium, and close to half of mined antimony. Gallium holds near $2,100 per kilogram outside China versus approximately $460 domestically — a roughly 4.5x premium. If the bans resume, Western semiconductor and defence supply chains face renewed disruption. Alcoa's Wagerup gallium refinery in Western Australia has taken FID but is not yet producing. Market participants are increasingly pricing in the probability of ban resumption.

watchItems.title: Trilateral summit aftermath — peace declaration but no Hormuz deliverables; G20 this weekend
watchItems.text: The Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral summit in Shenzhen produced a symbolic 'peace declaration' committing to nuclear risk reduction and ongoing dialogue — a diplomatic first — but no concrete deliverables on Hormuz, the November 27 critical minerals deadline, or Ukraine. The optics were historic but markets saw through to the substance gap. The G20 summit in Rio de Janeiro convenes this weekend (November 21–22), providing a follow-on venue for bilateral sidelines. Any Hormuz progress there could shift energy and helium markets; continued inaction raises the probability of further escalation, particularly after Thursday's mine incident.

watchItems.title: Anthropic ANT first week of trading — $97 close, +17% debut; Nasdaq-100 fast-track expected
watchItems.text: Anthropic (ANT) closed its first day of Nasdaq trading at $97, up 17% from its $83 opening price and well above the $70–$78 IPO pricing range. The stock briefly touched $102 intraday. The seven-partner chip-and-cloud private placement ($26 billion in Class N shares) adds institutional anchoring. Analysts expect ANT to be fast-tracked into the Nasdaq-100 at the next rebalancing. The first week of trading will establish whether the IPO pop holds or fades — lockup provisions, secondary offerings and analyst initiation coverage are the near-term catalysts. ANT's performance is a bellwether for the broader AI sector valuation narrative.

watchItems.title: Hormuz escalation — IRGC mines on tankers amid trilateral summit; three US carriers remain in Gulf
watchItems.text: Iran's IRGC planted mines on two tankers transiting the American-backed southern route on Thursday — the most provocative Hormuz escalation in weeks, timed to coincide with the trilateral summit. No casualties were reported but the incident drove Brent 2.0% higher to $92.00 and underscored the fragility of the southern corridor. Three US carrier strike groups remain in the Persian Gulf — the heaviest naval concentration since 2003. The mine incident raises the risk premium across energy, sulfur, helium and shipping markets. Total Hormuz incidents now exceed 135 since the crisis began.

desk.name: Gold
desk.m: 9th consecutive decline · lowest since Feb · down ~12% from Oct high · 10Y yield 5.10% · dollar near 19-month high · Dec hike odds 95%
desk.sum: Gold fell for a ninth straight session on Thursday, dropping 2.0% to $3,648 per ounce — the longest losing streak in over a year and the lowest level since February. The continued decline came despite the trilateral summit, as the symbolic peace declaration failed to shift the macro headwinds. The dollar held near its 19-month high and December rate-hike odds remained at 95%. The 10-year Treasury yield at 5.10% continues to make non-yielding gold expensive to hold. Central bank buying remains structurally supportive but insufficient to offset the yield and dollar pressure. The November 27 critical minerals deadline is now 7 days away. Key support at $3,600.

desk.name: Silver
desk.m: Continued losses · gold-silver ratio ~82 · down ~26% from Oct peak · industrial demand concerns weigh
desk.sum: Silver fell 1.7% to $44.44 per ounce on Thursday, extending losses as the FOMC-driven sell-off continued across precious metals. The gold-silver ratio holds near 82. Silver's dual precious-industrial profile leaves it vulnerable to both rising yields and slowing industrial activity signals. The trilateral summit's lack of concrete deliverables did little to shift sentiment. December rate-hike odds at 95% and the dollar near 19-month highs maintain a hostile macro environment. The break below $45 opens the next support zone around $43–$44.

desk.name: Oil
desk.m: WTI $82.50 · Iran mines on tankers · 3 US carriers in Gulf · summit no Hormuz deal · EIA crude build confirmed
desk.sum: Brent crude rebounded 2.0% to $92.00 per barrel on Thursday after Iran's IRGC planted mines on two tankers transiting the American-backed southern route — the most provocative Hormuz escalation in weeks. The incident was timed to coincide with the trilateral summit, which produced no Hormuz ceasefire framework. WTI slipped 1.9% to $82.50 as the EIA confirmed a large US crude inventory build. Three US carrier strike groups remain in the Persian Gulf. The divergence between Brent (rising on geopolitical risk) and WTI (falling on domestic oversupply) underscores the split in global oil dynamics.

desk.name: Copper
desk.m: LME ~$12,369/t · continued losses · DRC bridge disruption ongoing · dollar pressure · LME inventories elevated
desk.sum: Copper fell 2.4% to $5.61 per pound (approximately $12,369 per tonne LME) on Thursday, extending losses as the strong dollar and elevated LME inventories continued to pressure prices. The DRC bridge collapse continues to disrupt logistics, with alternative routes adding substantial time and cost. Emergency road assessments are ongoing. The trilateral summit produced no progress on trade policy that might have eased copper flows. AI data-centre, EV and electrification demand remain structural long-term drivers, but the hostile macro environment caps near-term upside.

desk.name: Coal
desk.m: Up ~40% YTD · held steady again · LNG JKM rolled to ~$27.50 · winter demand · no Hormuz deal from summit
desk.sum: Newcastle coal held at $150 per tonne on Thursday, continuing to buck broader commodity weakness as winter demand and the Hormuz-driven LNG supply crisis sustain the thermal fuel bid. Coal is up approximately 40% year to date. The trilateral summit produced no Hormuz ceasefire framework, extending the energy supply crisis. QatarEnergy's force majeure continues through at least end-December 2026. The LNG JKM front-month rolled to around $27.50, and the Iran mine incident on tankers reinforced the case for coal-to-gas substitution through winter.

desk.name: Platinum
desk.m: Modest decline after Wednesday's 4.8% crash · EV shift weighing · South African supply constrained · yields headwind
desk.sum: Platinum dipped 0.7% to $1,347 per ounce on Thursday, a modest follow-through decline after Wednesday's 4.8% crash. The EV transition continues to pressure automotive catalyst demand. South African mine supply remains constrained by ongoing power issues. With the dollar near a 19-month high and December rate-hike odds at 95%, the macro environment remains hostile. The trilateral summit's symbolic peace declaration did little for precious metals. Hydrogen electrolysis demand provides a structural long-term floor.

desk.name: Palladium
desk.m: Deep below $1,000 · down ~34% YoY · EV transition headwind dominant · weakest sustained level since 2018
desk.sum: Palladium fell 2.0% to $916 per ounce on Thursday, extending further below the $1,000 level. This remains the weakest sustained level since 2018. The structural headwind from the EV transition — battery EVs require no catalytic converter — continues to dominate. With the dollar near 19-month highs, yields at 5.10% and December rate-hike odds at 95%, the macro environment remains hostile. Tight South African mine supply offers limited support. The summit's peace declaration had no impact on palladium's structural bearish trend.

desk.name: Hormuz Terminal
desk.m: IRGC mines on 2 tankers Thu · summit no Hormuz deal · 3 US carriers in Gulf · 135+ total incidents · peace declaration only symbolic
desk.sum: The Strait of Hormuz crisis escalated on Thursday as Iran's IRGC planted mines on two tankers transiting the American-backed southern route — the most provocative incident in weeks, timed to coincide with the trilateral summit. No casualties were reported but Brent crude surged 2.0% on the news. The Trump–Xi–Putin summit produced a symbolic peace declaration but no Hormuz ceasefire framework. Three US carrier strike groups remain in the Persian Gulf — the heaviest concentration since 2003. Total incidents now exceed 135. The mine attack underscored that the southern corridor remains fragile and the crisis is far from resolved despite diplomatic efforts.

desk.name: Corn
desk.m: Modest decline · dollar strength persists · WASDE tighter balance sheet · South American planting favourable
desk.sum: December corn edged down to approximately 433 cents per bushel on Thursday, a modest 0.6% decline as dollar strength continued to weigh on US export competitiveness. The sell-off pace slowed markedly after Wednesday's 2.5% plunge. The USDA's tighter balance sheet from the November WASDE report provides a structural floor. South American planting continues under generally favourable conditions. The trilateral summit's lack of trade-policy progress leaves the Busan truce soybean commitments and broader grain flows unchanged. The November 27 deadline adds geopolitical uncertainty.

desk.name: Wheat
desk.m: Rebounded after consecutive days of selling · SovEcon Russia estimate supports floor · export demand picking up at lower levels
desk.sum: December wheat rebounded to approximately 577 cents per bushel on Thursday, up 1.2%, snapping back after consecutive days of heavy selling that had pushed prices to their lowest since January. Bargain buying emerged at the depressed levels. SovEcon's Russian wheat export estimate of 36 million tonnes — below the USDA's 39 million tonne forecast — provides a structural floor. Export demand picked up at the lower price levels. The trilateral summit and APEC meeting produced no progress on the Abu Dhabi grain corridor. The dollar remains a headwind but the worst of the selling pressure appears to have eased.

desk.name: Soybean
desk.m: January front-month ~$12.13 · modest decline · summit no Busan progress · South American supply competitive
desk.sum: January soybeans edged down to approximately 1,212¾ cents per bushel on Thursday, a modest 0.4% decline. The trilateral summit produced no visible progress on the Busan truce soybean commitments, which require China to purchase at least 25 million tonnes per year through 2028. South American supplies remain more competitive at current exchange rates. The USDA's tighter balance sheet from the WASDE report provides a structural floor. The dollar near 19-month highs remains a headwind for US exports. The G20 summit this weekend provides another venue for trade discussions.

desk.name: Cryptocurrencies
desk.m: ETH $1,802 · recovery from 200-week MA breakdown · Fear & Greed ticked up from Extreme Fear · ANT $97 debut · $260B+ wiped this month
desk.sum: Bitcoin recovered 2.2% to approximately $63,800 on Thursday, bouncing from oversold levels after Wednesday's break below the 200-week moving average. Ethereum rose 2.8% to $1,802. The Fear and Greed Index ticked up from Extreme Fear. Anthropic (ANT) closed its first day at $97, up 17% — the strong debut may partially offset the liquidity-drain narrative as institutional capital flows into AI. Spot Bitcoin ETF flows stabilised. Key resistance at $65,000 for Bitcoin; support at $61,000–$62,000. The macro headwinds from the FOMC remain, with December rate-hike odds at 95%.

desk.name: LNG
desk.m: JKM front-month rolled from Nov to Dec contract · apparent drop from $33 reflects rollover · TTF ~$29 · HH ~$3.25 · QatarEnergy FM continues · no Hormuz deal
desk.sum: The Asian LNG spot JKM front-month rolled from the expiring November contract to December, with the new front-month settling around $27.50 per MMBtu. The apparent decline from $33 reflects the contract rollover rather than a fundamental price drop — December delivery has always traded at a discount to the November squeeze. TTF sits near $29 per MMBtu; Henry Hub at $3.25. QatarEnergy's force majeure extends through at least end-December 2026. The trilateral summit produced no Hormuz ceasefire framework, and Thursday's mine incident on tankers reinforced the supply crisis. Winter demand remains the key driver through year-end.

desk.name: Sulfur
desk.m: FOB Kuwait ~$765 · 3 carriers in Gulf · summit no Hormuz deal · Iran mines on tankers · 7 days to Nov 27 deadline
desk.sum: Sulfur remains elevated at approximately $1,200 per tonne CFR Southeast Asia. The trilateral summit produced no Hormuz ceasefire framework, and Thursday's IRGC mine incident on tankers underscored the ongoing disruption to Middle Eastern supply logistics. Three US carrier strike groups remain in the Gulf. FOB Kuwait holds near $765 (KPC). The November 27 export-control deadline is now 7 days away. The G20 summit this weekend provides another diplomatic venue, but expectations for sulfur supply normalisation remain low.

desk.name: Potash
desk.m: BPC India $383 CFR · China benchmark ~$348 · summit no trade progress · G20 this weekend
desk.sum: Muriate of potash (MOP) CFR Brazil holds at approximately $358 per tonne. BPC's India contract remains approximately $25 above China's 2026 benchmark at $383 per tonne CFR. The trilateral summit produced no progress on trade policy or fertiliser flows. The G20 summit this weekend provides another venue. Belarus and Russia still account for about 40% of global supply despite Western sanctions. Wheat's Thursday rebound is modestly positive for near-term fertiliser demand sentiment after Wednesday's sharp sell-off.

desk.name: Antimony
desk.m: 7 days to Nov 27 deadline · Rotterdam $18,300–19,000/t · summit no progress on critical minerals
desk.sum: Chinese antimony (#1 ingot) holds near 93,500 yuan per tonne. Overseas antimony sits at approximately $18,300–19,000 per tonne in Rotterdam. The November 27 deadline is now 7 days away. Thursday's trilateral summit — the last major diplomatic window — produced no visible progress on critical minerals. Market participants are increasingly pricing in the probability of ban resumption. If the deadline passes without extension, overseas prices could spike further. China produces close to half of global mined antimony. The G20 this weekend is a last-chance venue for bilateral discussions.

desk.name: Gallium & Germanium
desk.m: Up >130% since early 2025 · 7 days to Nov 27 deadline · China domestic Ga ~$460/kg · summit no progress · ban resumption increasingly priced in
desk.sum: Gallium holds near $2,100 per kilogram outside China, with Chinese domestic gallium at approximately $460 per kilogram — a roughly 4.5x premium. Thursday's trilateral summit produced no progress on critical minerals, leaving the November 27 deadline now 7 days away with ban resumption increasingly priced in. China produces approximately 99% of global gallium and 60–80% of germanium. The underlying licensing regimes remain in force during the suspension. Alcoa's Wagerup gallium refinery has taken FID but is not yet producing. The G20 this weekend provides a final diplomatic venue.

desk.name: Vanadium
desk.m: Steady at $5.30 · upstream tightness · VRFB adoption timeline uncertain · China-Russia-SA control 90%+ · summit no progress on minerals
desk.sum: Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) holds at approximately $5.30 per pound in Europe, supported by persistent upstream tightness. The trilateral summit produced no visible progress on superhard materials or broader mineral restrictions. The long-term bull case rests on vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs) for grid-scale energy storage, but large-scale adoption timing remains uncertain. China, Russia and South Africa control over 90% of supply. The November 27 deadline, now 7 days away, affects the broader critical minerals complex.

desk.name: Cocoa
desk.m: Rebounded from $5,027 · West African supply concerns reasserted · ICE inventories elevated but fears persist · El Niño risk
desk.sum: ICE cocoa rebounded 2.8% to approximately $5,169 per tonne on Thursday, snapping back from Wednesday's 3% decline as renewed West African supply concerns reasserted themselves. Despite ICE warehouse inventories at a 2.5-year high of 3.8 million bags, the market remains focused on forward supply risks. Ivory Coast's Sodexam projection that 2026/27 output could drop 21–25% due to an 'exceptionally strong El Niño event' continues to provide a medium-term bullish underpinning. The bounce from $5,027 suggests the $5,000 level is acting as strong psychological support.

desk.name: Cobalt
desk.m: Declined from $35,000 · European demand concerns persist · Rotterdam $16–17/lb · DRC bridge disruption ongoing · NMC-to-LFP shift weighing
desk.sum: Cobalt is estimated near $33,525 per tonne, declining from approximately $35,000 as European demand concerns persist per Argus Media. Rotterdam standard-grade cobalt metal sits at $16–17 per pound. The DRC bridge collapse continues to have secondary effects on cobalt logistics from the same mining region, with alternative routes adding time and cost. The NMC-to-LFP battery chemistry shift weighs on the structural demand outlook. The dollar near 19-month highs adds to the headwinds for an already-weak market.

desk.name: Lithium
desk.m: Gave back Wednesday's rebound · structural oversupply persists · Goldman: 444k t global surplus by 2028 · monthly change -10%+
desk.sum: Chinese lithium carbonate pulled back to approximately ¥89,000 per tonne, giving back Wednesday's rebound as the broader commodity sell-off continued to weigh on sentiment. Structural oversupply remains the dominant theme, with Goldman Sachs projecting a 444,000-tonne global surplus by 2028. Lithium is down more than 10% over the past month. The EU's plan to cap Chinese EV imports at 350,000 units per year adds a demand headwind. Supply ramp-ups in Australia and South America continue to outpace demand growth. The ¥85,000–¥88,000 zone represents next major support.

desk.name: Rubber
desk.m: $2.55/kg · SE Asia supply tight · fungal blight ongoing · oil rebound modestly supports synthetic costs
desk.sum: Natural rubber (RSS3) trades near $2,550 per tonne ($2.55/kg), range-bound. Southeast Asian supply remains tight, with Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia — producing 70% of global latex — still affected by Pestalotiopsis fungal leaf blight. Thursday's Brent rebound to $92 modestly supports synthetic rubber production costs, tilting the balance slightly toward natural rubber. Auto-sector demand remains solid, supported by replacement-tyre cycles. The dollar near 19-month highs remains a headwind for dollar-denominated commodities.

desk.name: Uranium
desk.m: Spot eased slightly from $91 · long-term contracts near $99/lb · IAEA: 78 reactors under construction · AI demand structural
desk.sum: Uranium spot eased slightly to $90.22 per pound U₃O₈, with long-term contract prices near record US levels of $99 per pound — approaching the $100 milestone. The IAEA counts 78 reactors under construction worldwide and has raised its outlook for global nuclear capacity. Kazatomprom's TQZ sulphuric acid plant delays continue to limit leaching capacity. AI data-centre power demand remains a structural driver, with Meta, Amazon and Microsoft having signed nuclear power agreements. The slight decline reflects minor profit-taking rather than any fundamental shift.

desk.name: Rare Earths
desk.m: Ex-China NdPr $109–121/kg FOB · summit no progress on mineral controls · Nov 27 deadline 7 days · ban resumption increasingly priced in
desk.sum: Neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) oxide holds at approximately $73 per kilogram domestically in China, with ex-China prices at $109–121 per kilogram FOB. The trilateral summit produced no progress on critical mineral export controls. The November 27 US-specific deadline for gallium, germanium and antimony — now 7 days away — adds uncertainty to the broader critical minerals complex. Market participants are increasingly pricing in ban resumption. The G20 this weekend provides a final diplomatic venue for critical mineral discussions.
desk.src: SMM · Rare Earth Exchanges · Benchmark Minerals

desk.name: Manganese
desk.m: South Africa 37% · Gabon 18% · miners holding firm pricing stance · CIF China flat
desk.sum: Manganese ore (44% Mn content) trades near $4.40 per dry metric tonne unit CIF China, flat. Miners continue holding a firm pricing stance. South Africa supplies about 37% of global ore and Gabon 18%. Steel production consumes 90% of manganese demand. The forward cost picture provides support, but soft downstream consumption and the broader commodity sell-off cap near-term gains. The trilateral summit had no direct impact on manganese markets.

desk.name: Nickel
desk.m: Gave back Wednesday's gain · Indonesian RKAB uncertainty persists · global surplus continues · macro headwinds dominant
desk.sum: LME nickel fell 1.2% to $15,665 per tonne on Thursday, giving back Wednesday's modest gain as the broader macro headwinds reasserted. Indonesian RKAB mining quota uncertainty persists — potential tightening provides a floor while the global nickel surplus from Indonesian NPI and HPAL expansions caps upside. The trilateral summit and APEC trade talks produced no visible impact on nickel-relevant policy. The dollar near 19-month highs remains a headwind for dollar-denominated base metals.

desk.name: Tin
desk.m: Sharp decline · LME backwardation wide · Myanmar ban constraining supply · macro sell-off dominant · cancelled warrants elevated
desk.sum: LME tin fell approximately 4.4% to around $43,500 per tonne on Thursday, the steepest decline among base metals as the macro sell-off continued. Structural supply constraints persist from Myanmar's Wa State mining ban and Indonesian export licensing tightness. The LME backwardation remains wide, signalling tight near-term supply. However, macro pressure from the strong dollar and rising yields continues to overwhelm supply-side support. The November 27 deadline adds geopolitical uncertainty to the broader metals complex.

desk.name: Zinc
desk.m: Modest rebound after 4-day losing streak · Chinese smelter restart supply pressure easing · TCs deeply negative · structural deficit intact
desk.sum: LME zinc rose 0.9% to $3,562 per tonne on Thursday, a modest rebound after a four-day losing streak that had pushed prices to the lowest since late July. Bargain buying emerged at depressed levels. Treatment charges remain deeply negative, forcing continued smelter curtailments outside China. The structural supply deficit remains intact despite near-term macro pressure. Zinc is still up approximately 18% year-over-year. The dollar near 19-month highs remains a headwind but the worst of the recent selling appears to have eased.

desk.name: Tungsten
desk.m: Rotterdam APT $2,750 · China FOB $1,845 · Western ~3.5x China · 7 days to Nov 27 deadline · summit no progress
desk.sum: European tungsten APT holds at $2,750 per mtu in Rotterdam, while Chinese FOB sits at $1,845 per mtu — Western prices remain roughly 3.5 times Chinese domestic levels. The November 27 deadline is now 7 days away. The trilateral summit produced no visible progress on critical minerals. The market continues to reflect the fragmentation created by China's export controls. The G20 summit this weekend provides a final venue for bilateral discussions. If the bans resume next week, the Western premium could widen further.

desk.name: Helium
desk.m: Up 358% YTD · Ras Laffan repair 3–5 years · summit no Hormuz deal · Iran mines on tankers · IRGC escalation continues
desk.sum: Grade-A helium trades near $390 per thousand cubic feet, at critical levels. The trilateral summit produced no Hormuz ceasefire framework, and Thursday's IRGC mine incident on tankers escalated the crisis further. Three US carrier strike groups remain in the Gulf. QatarEnergy's Ras Laffan facility repairs remain estimated at 3–5 years. Qatar and the US together supply about 81% of global helium, and any path to restoring operations needs Hormuz de-escalation first. Russia's export controls extend through 2027. The G20 provides another diplomatic window but expectations are low.

desk.name: Phosphate
desk.m: OCP 30% global · DAP $560/t · sulfur cost surge pressuring economics · wheat rebound modestly positive for fertiliser
desk.sum: Phosphate rock trades near $120 per tonne FOB Morocco, with Morocco's OCP Group controlling about 30% of global trade. DAP prices sit near $560 per tonne CFR India. The sulfur price surge continues to pressure phosphate production economics. Thursday's wheat rebound to 577 cents is modestly positive for near-term fertiliser demand sentiment after Wednesday's sharp sell-off. The Hormuz crisis and Thursday's mine incident further reduce the probability of Middle Eastern sulfur supply normalising, keeping the cost structure elevated.

Newcastle coal held at $150 per tonne on Thursday, bucking broader commodity weakness as winter demand and the Hormuz-driven LNG supply crisis sustained the thermal fuel bid.

The November 27 deadline for China's export-control suspension on gallium, germanium and antimony is now 7 days away, and Thursday's trilateral summit produced no visible progress on critical minerals.
LME tin surged 4% on Thursday to $47,000 per tonne as Myanmar's Wa State lifted its mining ban, boosting supply expectations and triggering short covering across base metals.
Tin actually fell approximately 4.4% to around $43,500 per tonne — the steepest decline among base metals. Myanmar's Wa State mining ban remains in effect, continuing to constrain supply.
December wheat rebounded approximately 1.2% to 577 cents per bushel on Thursday, snapping back after consecutive days of heavy selling that had pushed prices to the lowest level since January.
